title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 65
paragraphs: That was all he said at the time. But about twenty days later he sent for the most distinguished of the Persians who were with him and spoke to them as follows: “Persians, I must now make known to you the thing I kept concealed beyond all others. While in Egypt I saw a vision in my sleep—would that I had never seen it. It seemed that a messenger came from home and reported to me that Smerdis was sitting on the royal throne and had touched the heavens with his head. Fearing I would be stripped of power by my brother, I acted quickly rather than wisely. For it seems no man can avert what is fated to happen. Fool that I was, I sent Prexaspes off to Susa to kill Smerdis. And once this great evil had been done, I lived in security, never considering the danger that some other man might one day rise up against me now that Smerdis had been removed. Missing the mark altogether of what was to happen, I both made myself the murderer of my brother—when there was no need—and have nonetheless been stripped of the kingdom. For it was Smerdis the Magian whom the divine power had foretold in the vision would rise up against me. So this deed has been done by me, and you must imagine that Smerdis son of Cyrus is no longer alive. In truth it is the Magians who are masters of your kingdom—the one I left as guardian of my household and his brother Smerdis. The man who above all others ought to have taken vengeance on my behalf for the dishonour I have suffered from the Magians has met an unholy death at the hands of his own nearest kin. And since he is no more, the next best thing I can do is to charge you, O Persians, with what I desire be done for me as I die. I lay this upon you, calling on the gods of the royal house to witness—on you, and most of all on those Achaemenids who are present here—that you do not allow the chief power to return to the Medes. If they have acquired it by craft, let them be deprived of it by craft in turn by you; if they have conquered it by force, then by force and a strong hand you must recover it. If you do this, may the earth bring forth her produce, and may your wives and your cattle be fruitful, while you remain free forever. But if you do not recover the power or attempt to recover it, I pray the opposite curses fall upon you, and moreover that every Persian meet an end to his life like the one that has come upon me.” As soon as Cambyses had finished speaking, he began to bewail and lament all his misfortunes.
